title: API Operational Cheatsheet — Timeouts, 429s, Streaming Degradation
content:
Summary and intent:
This is a working runbook / cheatsheet for on-call engineers at Redwood Inference to triage and mitigate the four most common API failure modes we see in production: client-observed timeouts, spikes of 429 rate-limit responses, degraded streaming (slow or stalled token streams), and elevated 5xx/error-rate conditions.

This doc is intentionally concise — use it as a fast checklist during paging and then expand into incident notes. It is a draft: TODOs and follow-ups are captured at the end.

Quick triage (first 7 minutes) — universal steps for any API alert:
- Confirm alert details (alert name, start time, affected routes). Pull from PagerDuty/opsgenie and the alerting dashboard.
- Scope: identify whether the issue is global, region-specific, or customer-specific.
  - Query per-route metrics: tokens/s, requests/s, error-rate, p50/p95 latency.
  - Check Recent Deploys: any model or runtime change in the last 30 minutes? (CI/GitHub Actions -> Deploys)
- Rollback policy check: if a deploy is suspected and the deploy can be reverted safely, coordinate with release-engineering.
- Notify product/customer-success if customer(s) are impacted (use established slack channel #sre-incidents and the customer impacted template).

Route-specific playbooks
1) Client-observed request timeouts (requests failing client-side with socket/HTTP timeout)
- Likely causes: slow model inference (long tails), overloaded serving nodes, request queue growth/backpressure, network egress issues, or proxy timeouts.
- Immediate checks:
  - Dashboards: check per-cluster request queue length and per-GPU utilization (dashboards: "Serving -> Queues" and "Infra -> GPU Util").
  - Check server-side p95/p99 token latency for affected model. If p99 token latency is spiking, suspect model-side slowdown.
  - Inspect gateway/proxy timeouts in logs (gateway nginx/edge logs). Are there 502/504s?
- Hot mitigations (fast):
  - Increase fast-tier capacity (if Dedicated/burst allowed) or activate autoscaling policy for Serving pool; scaling may take 1–5 minutes.
  - Temporarily increase client-side timeouts is acceptable for non-PL critical traffic (coordinate with product).
  - If a single large prompt or unexpected prompt shape is causing tail, apply request-size filter in gateway to reject very-long requests with 400 and ask clients to retry with smaller inputs.
- Longer-term mitigations:
  - Add model/sequence length guardrails and add synthetic probes to detect long-tail prompt shapes.
  - Tune batching/circuit-breaker thresholds; consider enabling per-customer throttles for heavy users.

2) 429 Rate-limited responses (sharp rise in 429s)
- Likely causes: traffic spike, abuse (bad client), quota misconfiguration, or sudden drop in capacity leading to throttling.
- Immediate checks:
  - Query per-customer 429 counts and top source API keys. (dashboards: "API -> Rate Limits by Key")
  - Check quota service logs and rate-limiter service health (cpu, mem, error logs).
- Hot mitigations:
  - Apply emergency soft-limit increases for high-value customers if safe and capacity exists.
  - Temporarily raise global rate-limit thresholds or enable short grace windows for queued requests (risk: higher downstream load).
  - If abuse detected: block offending API key(s) or IP CIDR via WAF rules.
- Investigation notes:
  - Correlate with marketing / product events (campaigns, new SDKs, customers onboarding).
  - For a distributed storm (many small clients), consider adding a short randomized retry-after header to help smooth traffic.

3) Degraded streaming (slow token stream, stalled chunks, or frequent reconnects)
- Likely causes: backend generator slowdowns, connection intermediaries (proxies/timeouts), websocket/HTTP2 proxy flaps, or intermittent KV cache misses.
- Immediate checks:
  - Reproduce a streaming call from inside the cluster (curl or SDK) to see server behavior — does stream start then stall?
  - Check edge long-lived connection counts and websocket/HTTP2 error counters.
  - Inspect per-request token emission rates on serving nodes.
- Hot mitigations:
  - Fallback to non-streaming completion for high-priority customers (switch to single-response completion with larger timeout).
  - If proxy is suspected, failover to an alternate edge region via origin routing rules.
  - If KV-cache cold misses correlate with stalls, temporarily pin popular prefixes in cache and enable a warming policy.
- Longer-term fixes:
  - Add more robust keepalive and backpressure signals between gateway and runtime.
  - Improve streaming test harness and add synthetic streaming health-checks (end-to-end).

4) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes across routes or a single route)
- Likely causes: runtime bugs, model loading failures, dependency failures (datastores, key-value cache, config service), or resource starvation.
- Immediate checks:
  - Inspect error-class breakdown in logs (Nginx 5xx, Runtime-exception, Model-load-failure, OOM, RPC timeouts).
  - Correlate errors with recent config changes (feature flags, rollout policies) or infra incidents (node reimaging, autoscaler flaps).
- Hot mitigations:
  - If model-load failures: mark model unhealthy in control plane so traffic is routed to a fallback variant.
  - If dependency (e.g., config service) is failing, switch to read-only cached config or promote standby.
  - If OOMs on nodes, drain and reprovision with larger instance type or reduce max-concurrent-requests.

Useful commands and quick queries (examples)
- k9s (cluster): check pods in namespace rwd-serving: kubectl -n rwd-serving get pods -o wide --show-labels
- Logs (ELK/Datadog): query: service:serving AND environment:prod AND response_status:[500 TO 599] | top 20 error_class
- Metrics (Prometheus): rate(api_responses_total{code="429"}[5m]) by (api_key)
- Check queue length: sum(serving_queue_length{cluster="prod"}) by (pool)

Escalation and communication
- Escalate to on-call SRE for infra if node provisioning / autoscaler behaviors are implicated.
- If root cause is model-related, page applied-ml and serving runtime leads.
- For pages impacting >1 major customer or extended (>30m) degradation, start an incident channel (#incident-<shortid>) and notify product + CS lead.

Post-incident follow up checklist (for incident review)
- Capture timeline (alerts, mitigation actions, communications).
- Identify the minimal change to prevent recurrence (hotfix, config guardrail, alert tuning).
- Add synthetic tests or blackbox probes where detection was slow.
- Review runbook gaps and update this doc with concrete commands and runbook snippets.

Notes-to-self (short list of actionables)
- Add a small internal endpoint that returns per-request serving-path traces (useful for quick triage without digging into logs).
- Add a Prometheus alert that triggers when p99 token latency AND queue_length are both elevated for >3m.
- Draft a customer-facing incident template for streaming degradations (so CS can copy/paste).

Open questions / TODOs
- Validate if any client SDK changes auto-retry aggressively and cause downstream storms — coordinate with devex.
- Determine clear thresholds for emergency quota increases (who authorizes, audit trail).
- Add sample curl commands for reproducing streaming issues from within each region.

Appendix: Short reproducible checks (copy/paste)
- Rapid 429 check: curl -s "https://api.redwood.ai/metrics/top-429-keys" | jq .
- Stream repro: curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"model":"rwd-translate","prompt":"hi","stream":true}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/responses

If you update this doc: please add your name + date at the bottom of the content and move any procedural steps that work into a permanent runbook in Confluence under SRE > Production Runbooks.
